children: Warren Buffett's decision to step down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway marks the end of an era on Wall Street. But judging by Berkshire's stock price, that era ended nearly 17 months ago.

The conglomerate's stock has yet to recover from the all-time high it hit on May 2 last year, the day before Buffett announced his plan to step down as CEO. Since then, Berkshire's popular Class B shares have slid 5.7%, versus a 34% rise in the S&P 500.

To be sure, there are several explanations for this divergence in performance. For one, Berkshire hasn't bet all that heavily on the AI boom that has driven U.S. indexes higher this year, although it has investments in tech names like Alphabet and Apple. Then there's Berkshire's big cash pile, which has also dragged on returns.

But how much of the stock performance is tied to Buffett's decision to step back? It's hard to quantify. Yet investors aren't rewarding today's announcement either. Berkshire's premarket activity suggests the stock will open slightly in the red.
